walkthroughs.body_html:
Genetics & Evolution HL — a core area of Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Genetics & Evolution HL brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Genetics & Evolution HL.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How many possible chromosome combinations from independent assortment in human gametes?

options: Prophase I of meiosis
Metaphase II
Anaphase II
Mitotic prophase

mcqs.q: Why is negative feedback the default mechanism in homeostasis?
options: Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.
It opposes deviations from a set point, returning the variable toward its normal value — keeping internal conditions stable.
Negative feedback amplifies changes to make them more noticeable.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.

mcqs.q: How does sweating help cool you down?
options: Sweat is cold and directly cools the skin on contact.
Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.
Evaporation of sweat absorbs energy (latent heat) from the skin, lowering body temperature.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.

mcqs.q: What reads the mRNA codons during translation?
options: tRNA molecules carrying specific amino acids — their anticodons pair with mRNA codons at the ribosome.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.
DNA directly reads the codons on mRNA and adds amino acids.
Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Homologous chromosomes”?
options: Two successive divisions producing four haploid gametes from one diploid cell; halves chromosome number.
Chromosomes of same length, centromere position and gene loci; one maternal, one paternal.
Photographic display of all chromosomes arranged in homologous pairs by size and banding.
Failure of homologues or chromatids to separate; causes aneuploidy (e.g., trisomy 21 in Down syndrome).
